title: Climbing the Warrior's Nose: A Sleeping Warrior Hike Above Lake Elementaita
meta_title: Sleeping Warrior Hike: 3 Summits and Glorious Lake Views
meta_description: Plan a sleeping warrior hike at Lake Elementaita: route over 3 summits, getting there from Nairobi, best months, safety and what to wear and pack.
excerpt: A practical sleeping warrior hike plan: the climb over the Warrior's nose, Ugali Hill and the Saucer, transport from Nairobi via Kikopey, the best dry months, safety around buffalo and the gear that grips loose volcanic soil.
content:
Seen from the Nairobi–Nakuru highway, the ridge above Lake Elementaita looks like a man asleep on his back, and a sleeping warrior hike takes you up over his face. Plan for 14-19 km, roughly 800 m of total climbing across three volcanic summits and six to seven hours on loose, thorny ground, about two hours' drive from Nairobi.

The route is short on shade, steep in two places and easy to underestimate because no summit tops 2,200 m. Below: the climb hill by hill, transport by car or matatu, the best months, what to wear and the safety points that matter on land shared with buffalo.

Quick Facts

  • Location: Kikopey, near Gilgil in Nakuru County, on Lake Elementaita's eastern shore by Soysambu Conservancy.
  • Distance from Nairobi: about 135-140 km, roughly 2 to 2.5 hours on the Nairobi–Nakuru highway.
  • Route length: 14 km for the shorter loop, up to about 19 km when Ugali Hill and the Saucer are added.
  • Altitude: about 1,780 m at the lake shore to about 2,110 m on the highest summit (one GPS record).
  • Time and difficulty: 6-7 hours of moving and resting; moderate to challenging, with two steep pitches.
  • Best months: the drier spells of January-February and June-September.

Where Is the Sleeping Warrior, and Why Is It Called That?

The Sleeping Warrior is a volcanic hill on the eastern shore of Lake Elementaita, in the Rift Valley between Naivasha and Nakuru. From the south, its profile resembles a reclining man, nose pointed at the sky.

Maasai tradition tells of a young moran, Olekibegelenya, who lay down for a nap after a feast of meat, milk and blood and never woke up. His age-mates could not wake him, and he became the hill. Colonial settlers called it "Delamere's Nose", after the family whose Soysambu ranch, today a conservancy of about 48,000 hectares, surrounds much of the lake.

The setting is half the appeal of a sleeping warrior hike. Lake Elementaita is one of three lakes in the Kenya Lake System World Heritage Site, listed in 2011 together with Nakuru and Bogoria, and the IUCN's World Heritage Outlook assessment says it holds the region's main breeding colony of great white pelicans. The lake is managed by the Kenya Wildlife Service as a wildlife sanctuary, so flamingos, pelicans and zebra are part of the scenery most days.

How Do You Get to the Sleeping Warrior Hike From Nairobi?

Take the A104 north-west from Nairobi towards Nakuru, pass Gilgil, and look for the Kikopey sign and its roadside nyama choma stalls. Tracks run from there to the lake shore below the hill.

By car

Leave the city by 6:00 am. Weekend traffic through Kikuyu builds quickly, and a late start pushes the steepest climbing into the midday heat. From the Kikopey turnoff the last stretch is murram, slippery after rain, so a car with decent clearance helps in the wet months.

By matatu

For a sleeping warrior hike without a car, Nakuru-bound matatus leave Nairobi's CBD through the morning. Tell the conductor you are going to Kikopey before you board, expect to pay the Nakuru fare, and arrange a boda boda from the roadside to the start. Keep the rider's number for the trip back.

The Sleeping Warrior Hike Route, Hill by Hill

The usual route starts on the lake shore, climbs the Warrior's face first, drops into a saddle, then climbs Ugali Hill and its flat-topped neighbour, the Saucer, before descending back towards Elementaita.

SectionWhat to expectRough time
Lake shore to the baseFlat, dusty tracks past acacia; birds in the shallows45-60 min
Up the "nose"Steepest pitch of the day, loose volcanic soil and rock1-1.5 hours
Saddle to Ugali HillDescent, then a second steep, thorny climb1.5-2 hours
Ugali SaucerThe highest point of the day, about 2,110 m on one GPS track30-45 min
Descent to the lakeLong, loose downhill; hard on knees1.5-2 hours

Figures vary because groups link the hills differently. One recorded GPS track of a sleeping warrior hike came to 18.7 km in about six hours twenty minutes, with 818 m of ascent between roughly 1,782 m and 2,110 m. Other descriptions give 14 km and six to eight hours. Treat it as a full day.

The lake shore and hot springs

The first hour of a sleeping warrior hike is gentle and the best time for photographs, with low light on the water and birds in the shallows. Some groups finish at the small hot springs on the shore, too shallow to swim in but good for tired feet.

Climbing the Warrior's nose

The nose is short and very steep, on gravelly soil that rolls under your boots. Take small steps and leave a gap behind the person in front so loose stones miss them. From the top, Elementaita spreads out below you.

Ugali Hill and the Saucer

Ugali Hill is named for its rounded shape, but its climb is the thorniest part of a sleeping warrior hike, with acacia and low scrub snagging bare legs, and as steep as the nose. Many groups pass the Lord Cole monument, a colonial-era memorial overlooking the lake, on this stretch or on the way down.

When Is the Best Time for a Sleeping Warrior Hike?

January-February and June-September are the best months to climb the Warrior, when roads and slopes are dry. The long rains (roughly March-May) and short rains (roughly October-December) make the loose soil greasy and the access tracks muddy.

On a sleeping warrior hike, time of day matters as much as the month. The valley floor warms up fast and there is almost no shade above the shore. Start walking by 8:00 am, aim to be past the steepest climbs before noon, with a light layer for the summit wind. In the short rains, watch for afternoon storms and come down early if the sky darkens.

What Should You Wear and Pack for the Sleeping Warrior Hike?

Wear boots with a deep, grippy sole, long trousers against thorns, a wide-brim hat and a breathable long-sleeve top, and carry at least 3 litres of water.

Trail shoes cope with the lake shore, but the descents of a sleeping warrior hike reward ankle support and lugs that bite into loose ground. A pair such as the Quechua waterproof hiking boot handles both the dust and the odd wet patch in the rainy months. Pair it with merino wool hiking socks, which handle sweat better than cotton and cut the risk of blisters on the long downhill.

Water is what people get wrong. There is nowhere to refill on a sleeping warrior hike, so a 3L hydration backpack lets you sip on the steep pitches without stopping. On top, a wide-brim safari hiking sun hat protects your neck and ears from equatorial sun that feels milder than it is when the wind blows.

Pro Tips for the Day

  • Start early: be on the trail by 8:00 am so the two steep climbs of a sleeping warrior hike are behind you before midday.
  • Pack 3 litres: there is no water on the route, and the descent is where people run dry.
  • Cover your legs: zip-off or light trousers save your shins from acacia thorns.
  • Use poles on the way down: loose volcanic soil on the descent is harder than the climb.
  • Plan your ride home: agree a pick-up time at Kikopey before you start walking.

Is the Sleeping Warrior Hike Safe?

Sleeping Warrior is safe for fit walkers who go in a group, with a local guide, in daylight. The real hazards are heat, dehydration, loose ground on the descents and the large animals of Soysambu.

Buffalo live on the conservancy, and a lone bull in thick bush is the animal to respect most. Walk with a guide who knows the area, keep well back from any buffalo or giraffe, and never edge closer for a photo.

Parts of the route cross conservancy land and the lake is a Kenya Wildlife Service sanctuary, so confirm current fees and whether a guide is required with the Kenya Wildlife Service and the conservancy before you travel. Carry ID, some cash and a charged phone.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long is the sleeping warrior hike?

The full route usually covers 14-19 km, depending on whether your group adds Ugali Hill and the Saucer to the Warrior itself. Most groups take six to seven hours including rests, and one recorded GPS track was 18.7 km with 818 m of total climbing. Allow extra time for photos, the loose descents and the drive back to Nairobi.

Is Sleeping Warrior hard for beginners?

A sleeping warrior hike suits beginners who already walk regularly, but it is harder than its modest height suggests. Two very steep climbs on loose soil, little shade and a long downhill make it tougher than Ngong Hills or Karura. Anyone who has managed a full day on Longonot or Kilimambogo will usually cope well with a guide and an early start.

How far is Elementaita from Nairobi?

Lake Elementaita is roughly 135-140 km from Nairobi along the Nairobi–Nakuru highway, about two to two and a half hours by car depending on traffic around Kikuyu and Naivasha. The Kikopey turnoff near Gilgil is the usual landmark for the Sleeping Warrior trailhead, and Nakuru-bound matatus can drop you there.

Do you need a guide for the sleeping warrior hike?

A guide is strongly advised here because paths across the hills are faint, the area is home to buffalo, and parts of the route cross conservancy land. Confirm current guide and entry requirements with the Kenya Wildlife Service and the conservancy before your trip, as arrangements can change.

Can I swim at the Elementaita hot springs after the hike?

The Elementaita hot springs are too shallow for swimming, but you can soak your feet or splash warm water on your legs after a sleeping warrior hike. They sit on the lake shore and make a relaxed end to the day. Do not drink the water, keep away from feeding birds, and pack a small towel and dry socks.

Final Thoughts

Three short, sharp climbs above a soda lake full of birds make a rare day out within two hours of the city.

Go in the dry months, start before the heat, wear boots that grip loose soil and carry more water than you think. Do that and the sleeping warrior hike becomes one of the best walks in the central Rift Valley. Pick a date, gather your group and sort your kit this week.
